name: Abishua
title: Priest in the lineage of Aaron through Phinehas
lifespan: Unknown, likely the period of the judges
summary: Abijah belonged to the priestly lineage that went from Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas. Although his individual deeds are not described in the Bible, he plays a central genealogical role as a link between the early high priests and later figures such as Zadok and Ezra. In Ezra's family tree, he serves as an important link confirming the unbroken priestly inheritance from Aaron, which was of great significance for legitimizing the priestly service after the return from Babylon. Through his place in the genealogies, Abijah testifies to God's faithfulness in maintaining the priesthood through generations.

keyEvents.title: Listed in the priestly genealogy
keyEvents.description: Abishua is mentioned as the son of Phinehas and father of Bukki in the priestly genealogy in 1 Chronicles. This list documents the unbroken line of high priests from Aaron through Eleazar and onward through the generations.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Ezra's genealogy
keyEvents.description: In Ezra's genealogy, Abishua is listed as a link between Phinehas and Bukki. This genealogy serves to confirm Ezra's priestly authority and his right to lead the religious restoration after returning from the Babylonian exile.

keyEvents.title: Father of Bukki
keyEvents.description: Abishua had a son named Bukki, who continued the priestly lineage. Through this line, the high priesthood was passed down toward later central figures such as Zadok in David's time and Ezra after the exile.

versions.summary: Abishua was a descendant of Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas. He is mentioned in the priestly genealogies as an important link in the high-priestly line from Aaron to Ezra. His role in the Bible is primarily genealogical, but he represents continuity in the Levitical priesthood.
versions.title: Descendant of Aaron in the Priestly Line
versions.reason: [minor] Abishua likely lived during the conquest period or early judges period. 'conquest' is acceptable, but given the uncertainty around exact dating, 'judges' could also have been considered. 'conquest' is retained as reasonable.; [minor] The third and fourth key events overlap significantly with the first and second. The profile has five keyEvents that largely cover the same genealogical information. It could have been more consistent with fewer events.; [major] 1 Chron 6:4-5 and 6:50 refer to the priestly line, but verse numbering varies between different Bible translations. In some translations, this passage begins at 5:30 (Hebrew numbering) instead of 6:4. Verse 50 in 1 Chron 6 concerns Aaron's sons and the altars, not directly Abishua in all translations. Verse 50 should be verified; in many translations it is verses 4-5 that mention Abishua, while verse 50 mentions the Eleazar line in a parallel list. Retained but marked as potentially inaccurate.; [major] There are no footnotes providing historical, linguistic, or theological context about this person. Information should be added about the meaning of the name, the significance of the priesthood, and the function of genealogies.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could also mention that Abishua is named in Ezra's genealogy, which underscores his importance for post-exilic identity.

versions.summary: Abishua was a descendant of Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas. He is mentioned in the priestly genealogies as an important link in the high-priestly line from Aaron to Ezra. His role in the Bible is primarily genealogical, but he represents continuity in the Levitical priesthood. In Ezra 7, he is noted as part of Ezra's own lineage, which was crucial for legitimizing priestly service after the Babylonian exile.
versions.title: Descendant of Aaron in the Priestly Line
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (starting almost identically). It should be rephrased more to distinguish it from earlier versions.; [major] Abishua is primarily known from genealogical lists spanning many generations. His placement in the 'conquest' period is uncertain. Based on the lineage between Phinehas and Zadok (David's time), he could just as well be placed in the period of the judges ('judges'). Given that he was the son of Phinehas, who was active during the conquest period, 'judges' is a more likely timeframe for Abishua himself.; [minor] 'ca. 1400 BC' is very early. If Phinehas was active around 1400–1350 BC, Abishua would rather have been active around 1370–1350 BC or later, in the transition to the period of the judges. A broader indication such as 'ca. 1350 BC' or 'unknown' would be more precise.; [minor] The four events overlap thematically to some extent – especially event 1 and 2 both concern the priestly genealogy in 1 Chronicles 6. These could with advantage be merged or differentiated more clearly.; [minor] Verses 3–6 and 50–51 in 1 Chron 6 are a broad reference. Verse 3 concerns Aaron and his sons, not directly Abishua. It may be better to limit it to the verses that actually mention Abishua.

footnotes.text: The name Abishua (Hebrew: אֲבִישׁוּעַ) likely means "my father is salvation" or "my father is wealth/noble." It is composed of 'avi' (my father) and 'shua' (salvation/wealth), reflecting a theological confession common in Israelite personal names.

The priestly genealogies in 1 Chronicles 6 and Ezra 7 serve an important theological function by establishing an unbroken line from Aaron to the post-exilic priests, thereby legitimizing temple worship after the return from Babylon. Abishua serves as a key link in this chain.

In rabbinic tradition (e.g., Talmud, Bava Batra 109b), Abishua is mentioned in connection with the priestly line. Some Jewish sources from the Second Temple period attribute to him a role in preserving the holy priesthood during a turbulent period.

The priestly genealogy in 1 Chronicles has different verse numbering in the Hebrew text (5:27–6:38) compared to most translations (6:1–53). Readers should be aware that references may vary depending on which textual tradition is followed.

Abishua likely lived during the transition between the period of settlement and the period of the judges. The chronology for this period is debated among scholars, and the biblical genealogies may contain omissions of generations, making precise dating difficult.
